1.q: Which statement best defines a project?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a unique, defined outcome
A permanent department within the organisation's structure
A standard procedure that is repeated continuously over time
An ongoing operation that supports routine business functions
1.w: APM defines a project as a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to achieve planned objectives.

1.q: Which sequence best represents the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Initiation, sprint, retrospective, closure
Forming, storming, norming, performing
Concept, definition, deployment, transition
Concept, iteration, review, release
1.w: A linear life cycle runs sequentially through the concept, definition, deployment and transition phases.

1.q: What is the primary responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Maintaining and updating the project schedule daily
Owning the business case and securing the resources for the project
Producing the detailed technical deliverables
Carrying out the day-to-day management of project tasks
1.w: The sponsor is accountable for the business case and for ensuring the project is resourced and remains worthwhile.

1.q: What is meant by a deployment baseline?
o: The initial list of stakeholders identified for the project
The approved reference for scope, schedule and cost against which performance is measured
The final approved budget figure for the project
The agreed schedule of all the project's meetings
1.w: The deployment baseline is the approved version of the plan against which actual progress and performance are measured.

1.q: What is meant by scope management?
o: Selecting and managing the project's suppliers
Preparing and controlling the project's overall budget
Defining and controlling what is, and is not, included in the project
Scheduling the sequence in which tasks are carried out
1.w: Scope management defines the totality of the outputs and work required, and controls what is and is not included.

1.q: What is the main purpose of critical path analysis within a project schedule?
o: To identify the sequence of activities that determines the shortest project duration
To distribute resources evenly across all of the project's activities
To define the roles and responsibilities of the project team
To estimate the project's costs from comparable past projects
1.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the minimum overall duration of the project.

1.q: In the context of project management, how is the term 'risk' best defined?
o: A deliverable that has been completed and formally accepted
A certain event that will definitely disrupt the project's objectives
A problem that has already occurred and now requires resolution
An uncertain event that, if it occurs, could affect objectives positively or negatively
1.w: A risk is an uncertain future event or set of circumstances that, should it occur, would have an effect on the achievement of objectives.

1.q: In the context of a project, how is the term 'quality' best defined?
o: The degree to which the deliverables meet the agreed requirements
The speed at which the project's activities are completed
The number of features included within the final deliverables
The total amount of budget spent on producing the deliverables
1.w: Quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of the deliverables fulfils the agreed requirements.

1.q: Within the context of a project, how is the term 'communication' best defined?
o: The method used to estimate the project's overall budget
The exchange of information between stakeholders to help achieve the objectives
The process used to sequence the project's scheduled activities
The technique used to identify and assess the project's risks
1.w: Communication is the exchange of information so that the right stakeholders have the right information at the right time.

1.q: In the context of a project, how is the term 'leadership' best defined?
o: The set of fixed procedures the team is required to follow
The act of allocating tasks to individuals and doing nothing further
The ability to inspire, guide and influence a team towards its goals
The formal chart that shows the project's reporting lines
1.w: Leadership is the ability to establish vision and direction, and to inspire and influence people to achieve the project's goals.

1.q: How does project management differ from managing business-as-usual operations?
o: It manages repetitive work that continues indefinitely
It produces no deliverables of any kind
It manages unique, time-bounded work with a defined objective
It requires no resources to be committed to it
1.w: Project management delivers unique, temporary work, whereas business-as-usual is ongoing and repetitive.

1.q: Which statement best describes how work progresses in a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: Repeated cycles of planning, building and reviewing that refine the product incrementally
Predictive up-front planning combined with a one-off handover
A feasibility study followed only by long-term operational support
A single sequential pass through fixed phases from concept to closure
1.w: An iterative life cycle repeats build-and-review cycles, refining and adding to the product over successive iterations.

1.q: What is the main role of the project manager?
o: Owning and approving the project's business case
Setting the organisation's overall strategy
Managing the project day to day to deliver within its constraints
Providing the funding required for the project
1.w: The project manager is responsible for day-to-day management to deliver the objectives within time, cost and quality constraints.

1.q: How do deployment baselines typically differ between linear and iterative life cycles?
o: Linear baselines cover only scope, whereas iterative baselines cover only cost
Linear baselines change daily, whereas iterative baselines never change
Linear baselines are largely fixed, whereas iterative baselines are revisited each iteration
Linear baselines are optional, whereas iterative baselines are mandatory
1.w: A linear life cycle sets the baseline once, while an iterative life cycle re-baselines regularly as each iteration is planned.

1.q: How does scope management typically differ between iterative and linear project life cycles?
o: Iterative and linear life cycles both fix all scope before any work begins
Iterative life cycles fix scope early, whereas linear life cycles refine scope each phase
Iterative life cycles refine scope each cycle, whereas linear life cycles baseline scope early
Iterative life cycles ignore scope, whereas linear life cycles define it repeatedly
1.w: Iterative life cycles progressively elaborate scope across cycles, whereas linear life cycles baseline the scope once, early on.

1.q: What does resource levelling involve when a project schedule shows its resources to be over-allocated?
o: Adjusting activity dates so demand does not exceed availability, even if the end date moves
Increasing the budget so additional resources can be hired immediately
Scheduling all activities in parallel so resources are used at once
Reducing the project's scope so the existing resources become sufficient
1.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to keep demand within available resource limits, and may extend the project end date to do so.

1.q: What is the main purpose of a risk register on a project?
o: To allocate the project's budget across its individual work packages
To record identified risks together with their analysis, responses and current status
To define the agreed boundaries of the project's scope of work
To list the project's milestones and their planned completion dates
1.w: A risk register documents each identified risk with its assessment, planned response and status, supporting ongoing monitoring and control.

1.q: What is the main purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: To inspect each finished deliverable against its acceptance criteria
To provide confidence, by auditing the processes, that requirements will be met
To plan the sequence and timing of the project's activities
To define the agreed boundaries of the project's scope of work
1.w: Quality assurance audits processes and methods to give confidence that the project will meet its quality requirements.

1.q: Which of the following would typically be found within a project's communication plan?
o: The identified risks together with their planned responses
The decomposition of the final product into its components
Stakeholders' information needs and the methods used to meet them
The hierarchy of work packages making up the scope
1.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when, how and by whom it will be provided.

1.q: How can a project leader most effectively influence the performance of their team?
o: By focusing only on individual tasks rather than the shared goals
By taking every decision alone without seeking any input from others
By limiting communication so that the team can work undisturbed
By setting clear objectives, offering support and giving constructive feedback
1.w: Leaders raise performance by clarifying objectives, supporting the team and using constructive feedback to develop individuals.

2.q: An organisation must implement a new CRM system by December to improve sales tracking. Which term best describes this piece of work?
o: Project
Programme
Business-as-usual
Portfolio
2.w: It is a project: a unique, temporary undertaking with a defined end date and a specific deliverable.

2.q: A team plans the overall scope up front using a predictive approach, then builds the features in a series of iterative sprints. What life cycle is this?
o: Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
2.w: A hybrid life cycle combines predictive (linear) planning with iterative delivery of the work.

2.q: A senior director approves the budget and champions the project at board level. Which project role is this?
o: Product owner
End user
Project sponsor
Project manager
2.w: Championing the project and owning its funding and governance at a senior level is the role of the project sponsor.

2.q: A project manager decides which documents to fix as the reference for measuring future performance. What is being established?
o: Stakeholder register
Risk register
Communication plan
Deployment baseline
2.w: Fixing the agreed scope, schedule and cost documents as the reference point creates the deployment baseline.

2.q: Which structure decomposes a project's final output into its major products and their component parts?
o: Product breakdown structure (PBS)
Cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
Work breakdown structure (WBS)
2.w: A product breakdown structure hierarchically decomposes the end product into its major components and sub-components.

2.q: Which resource optimisation technique evens out resource usage by delaying tasks only within their available float?
o: Critical path analysis
Resource smoothing
Schedule crashing
Resource levelling
2.w: Resource smoothing delays activities within their float to even out resource usage while keeping the critical path and end date unchanged.

2.q: A key supplier unexpectedly ceases trading during delivery. How should this now be classified?
o: A risk, because it remains an uncertain future possibility
An opportunity, because it is likely to benefit the project
A change request, because it alters the project's agreed scope
An issue, because the uncertain event has now actually occurred
2.w: An issue is an event that has occurred and now requires management action, whereas a risk is still an uncertain future possibility.

2.q: A deliverable fails to meet its acceptance criteria during inspection. Which quality activity has identified this?
o: Quality planning
Quality control
Change control
Quality assurance
2.w: Quality control inspects and tests deliverables against their acceptance criteria to confirm whether they conform.

2.q: A sponsor asks for a progress update by email every Friday. Which element of the communication plan does this define?
o: The frequency and channel of the communication
The sourcing approach for external suppliers
The acceptance criteria for the deliverable
The sequence of the activities in the schedule
2.w: Specifying weekly delivery by email defines the frequency and the channel that the communication plan records for that stakeholder.

2.q: Conflict and disagreement emerge as a newly formed team begins working together. Which Tuckman stage does this describe?
o: Storming
Forming
Performing
Norming
2.w: In Tuckman's model, storming is the stage where interpersonal conflict and challenges to direction typically arise.

2.q: A team runs the same server backups every day as part of normal operations. How is this work best classified?
o: Portfolio
Business-as-usual
Project
Programme
2.w: Routine, repetitive and ongoing tasks such as daily backups are business-as-usual rather than a project.

2.q: A project includes a feasibility phase before delivery and a period of operational support after handover. Which life cycle term describes this?
o: Hybrid project life cycle
Iterative project life cycle
Linear project life cycle
Extended project life cycle
2.w: An extended life cycle adds pre-project and post-project phases, such as feasibility and operation, around the core life cycle.

2.q: A person is assigned to carry out the work packages defined in the plan and produce the outputs. Which role is this?
o: Product owner
Project sponsor
Project team member
Project manager
2.w: Project team members carry out the work packages and produce the deliverables set out in the plan.

2.q: Before any work begins the sponsor wants a document justifying the investment through its costs, benefits and risks. Which document is this?
o: Work breakdown structure
Risk register
Business case
Quality plan
2.w: The business case justifies the project by setting out its benefits, costs, risks and options to support the investment decision.

2.q: Which structure decomposes the total work of a project into manageable work packages?
o: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
Product breakdown structure (PBS)
Cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
2.w: A work breakdown structure breaks the project's deliverables down into a hierarchy of manageable work packages.

2.q: Which document sets out a project's approach to sourcing, including make-or-buy decisions and contract types?
o: Procurement strategy
Quality plan
Risk register
Communication plan
2.w: The procurement strategy defines how goods and services will be sourced, covering make-or-buy analysis, contract types and supplier selection.

2.q: You find the same fault recurring in every test cycle. Which process should be used to log and resolve it?
o: Quality planning
Risk identification
Scope definition
Issue management
2.w: Issue management logs, tracks and resolves problems that have already occurred and are affecting the project.

2.q: The project management office carries out an audit of whether the agreed processes are being followed. Which activity is this?
o: Quality control
Quality planning
Risk analysis
Quality assurance
2.w: Quality assurance uses audits of processes to verify that they are being applied correctly and meet the required standards.

2.q: A team member misreads a decision because tone and body language were absent. Which drawback of communication does this show?
o: Physical communication always reaches the wrong recipients
Virtual communication guarantees that every message is understood
Virtual communication can lose the non-verbal cues that face-to-face provides
Face-to-face communication prevents any written record being kept
2.w: Virtual communication without video removes the non-verbal cues available face-to-face, increasing the chance of misinterpretation.

2.q: You assign members to behavioural roles such as Coordinator, Plant and Completer Finisher. Which model are you applying?
o: Belbin's team roles
PESTLE analysis
Tuckman's stages of team development
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
2.w: Belbin's model identifies behavioural team roles, such as Coordinator and Plant, that contribute to a balanced, effective team.
